analysis.one_liner: Forces large credit card issuers to let merchants route transactions over competing payment networks.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on September 19, 2022, received no further action, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar banks with more than $100 billion in assets from requiring that credit card transactions run over just one or two payment networks. Merchants who accept credit cards could then choose among competing networks to process each sale, the way they already can for debit cards. The goal is to break into the Visa-Mastercard duopoly and drive down the 'interchange' fees merchants pay on every swipe — fees that are passed along in prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants — retailers, grocers, restaurants, gas stations — who pay a fee on every credit card sale and would gain leverage to route transactions through cheaper networks. Consumers could ultimately see some of the savings in prices, though the main direct beneficiary is the merchant side.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Federal Reserve to bar large card issuers (banks with over $100 billion in assets) from restricting transaction routing to one network, to affiliated networks, or to the two largest networks — in practice, Visa and Mastercard.

It prohibits issuers and networks from penalizing or restricting merchants who route transactions over other eligible networks, including penalties for failing to meet transaction-volume minimums on a particular network.
It directs the Federal Reserve and Treasury to publish a list of payment card networks that pose a national security risk or are owned or sponsored by a foreign state entity.

analysis.who_pays: The two dominant card networks (Visa and Mastercard) and the largest card-issuing banks, which collect interchange fees on every transaction and would face price competition on routing. Some consumers could see reduced credit card rewards, which are funded partly by those fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Visa, Mastercard, and big card-issuing banks

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only issuers with more than $100 billion in assets and exempts cards in a three-party model (such as American Express and Discover), leaving smaller issuers and those networks outside its reach.
The bill strips the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau of authority to enforce the new routing requirements, leaving enforcement with the Federal Reserve.

Opponents of routing mandates, including the card networks and large banks, argue that reduced interchange revenue would be made up through higher card fees and smaller rewards programs, and that less routing volume per network could weaken fraud-security investment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real but indirect for consumers: merchants pay billions in swipe fees and cheaper routing could push some of that back into prices. The main cost is that rewards programs, which wealthier cardholders use most, are funded by the same fees and could shrink. Exemptions for small banks and three-party networks limit disruption but also limit the competitive effect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee from the day it was introduced until Congress adjourned — no markup, no vote, never reached the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2022 on September 19, 2022, joined by Rep. Lance Gooden (R-TX).
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have required the Federal Reserve to prohibit large issuers from limiting transaction routing to one or two dominant networks and to bar penalties on merchants who choose other networks.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Visa, Mastercard, and the largest card-issuing banks keep the existing two-network routing structure and the interchange fees merchants pay on every credit card transaction. Merchants continue paying those fees, with no competing networks to route through.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Visa, Mastercard, and large card-issuing banks

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Lance Gooden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the sole cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Merchant Payments Coalition
for.role: Coalition of retail, grocery, restaurant, and convenience-store trade groups
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for routing competition in credit transactions, following the debit routing rules won in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill; it stayed at the referral stage until Congress ended.

against.name: Visa
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and funded campaigns against routing mandates, arguing they would reduce rewards and security.

against.name: Mastercard
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and lobbied against credit routing mandates alongside Visa.

against.name: Electronic Payments Coalition
against.role: Trade group for card networks and large banks
against.what_they_did: Ran opposition messaging against the bill on behalf of banks and networks.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two named sponsors were a Democrat (Welch of Vermont) and a Republican (Gooden of Texas), though the House version drew only one cosponsor before dying in committee.

industries.note: The two largest networks collect a fee on every credit card transaction and would lose their guaranteed duopoly over routing; merchants could route sales through cheaper competitors. Their interest in keeping fees high runs against merchants and ultimately consumers who pay prices that cover those fees.

Banks with over $100 billion in assets capture interchange revenue on the cards they issue and would lose the ability to lock routing to one or two networks. Smaller banks under the threshold are exempt.

Retailers, grocers, restaurants, and gas stations pay a percentage fee on every credit sale and would gain the ability to route transactions over cheaper networks, with the prospect of passing savings to customers.
Networks outside the top two would become eligible to process credit transactions on large issuers' cards, opening a market currently closed to them.
Cards in a three-party model — where the issuer is the network — are expressly exempt from the routing rules, leaving their closed-loop structure untouched.
